title: Measure Now, Mitigate Later: Virtual Error Cancellation for Logical Quantum Circuits
authors: Oles Shtanko, Saswata Roy, Shashwat Kumar, Zlatko Minev
abstract: Early fault-tolerant quantum algorithms are a key step in scalable quantum computing, but are ultimately constrained by residual, uncorrectable logical errors. Logical quantum error mitigation can eliminate this bias, however its standard requirements include prior noise characterization, more complex experiments, and substantial sampling overhead. Although no mitigation technique can simultaneously overcome all three constraints, we demonstrate that the first two---noise learning and need for modified circuits---can be completely bypassed for logical circuits by leveraging only syndrome records. Specifically, we introduce virtual error cancellation: a method that, unlike previous bias-free approaches, operates entirely in classical post-processing on universal quantum circuits. We develop and numerically test end-to-end protocols that reduce the sampling overhead beyond fundamental limitations of existing syndrome-aware mitigation techniques, including syndrome-based postselection. In particular, we propose a scheme that pairs the low-latency decoder used in the experiment with a high-complexity decoder run in post-processing. In numerical simulations of a distance-7 rotated surface code, we show that our full-stack dual-decoder algorithm exhibits an error that diminishes as the number of samples increases, capable of reaching more than three orders of magnitude of suppression compared to the decoded logical error rate in an experimentally achievable setting. These results establish syndrome records as a resource for correcting universal computational estimates after quantum execution.
summary: This paper introduces Virtual Error Cancellation (VEC), a novel post-processing technique to combat residual logical errors in quantum computation. VEC leverages syndrome records to estimate logical observables without requiring full noise characterization or circuit modification. The results demonstrate that this method achieves significant error suppression with a theoretically bounded and near-optimal sampling overhead.
main_problem: The primary challenge is mitigating residual, uncorrectable logical errors in early fault-tolerant quantum algorithms that persist even after physical error correction.
main_result: The proposed Virtual Error Cancellation (VEC) method allows for error suppression exceeding three orders of magnitude in simulations by operating entirely in classical post-processing using only syndrome records.
method: VEC is a novel classical post-processing technique that constructs an unbiased estimator by assigning weights to syndrome records, bypassing the need for prior noise characterization or circuit modification.
model_or_system: The analysis is performed on logical quantum circuits, specifically using the framework of stabilizer codes like the distance-7 rotated surface code.
key_observables: Logical Error Rate ($p_L$), Sampling Overhead ($C(w)$), Syndrome Record ($s$), and the estimator $\hat{\langle O angle}_{	ext{VEC}}$.
important_parameters: Code distance ($d$), sampling overhead scaling factor ($\eta$), and the minimal weight difference ($\Delta W_{min}$) characterizing error regimes.
main_assumptions: The physical noise is assumed to be described by a Pauli channel, and the analysis often relies on asymptotic expansions and the system operating below the error threshold ($p < p_{th}$).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the VEC concept, comparing sampling overhead scaling ($\eta$) against existing methods, and detail the dual-decoder architecture used for coarse-grained cancellation.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theory of unbiased estimators using syndrome records, derives optimal filter weights, introduces coarse-grained and dual-decoder protocols for tractability, and finally analyzes the scaling and residual error suppression in the decoupled limit.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, resource-efficient theoretical tool for quantifying and suppressing errors in quantum computation that is highly relevant to experimental quantum information scientists.
